title: The Inland Ewe States: Many Towns, One Voice

pages.text: On the ninth of May 1956, people lined up in towns and villages across the hills east of the River Volta. Each voter was given a paper and two choices. One was to join their land to the Gold Coast, which was about to become independent. The other was to stay apart for the time being, under the United Nations. Farmers, teachers, traders, and chiefs all voted. The result changed the map of West Africa and made this land a part of Ghana. To see why such a vote was needed, we must follow the story of the inland Ewe.

Farmers, teachers, traders, and chiefs all voted.

To see why such a vote was needed, we must follow the story of the inland Ewe.
pages.alt: A queue of men and women outside a small polling station in a hill town, each holding a slip of paper.

pages.text: When the Ewe left Notsie, some went to the coast and founded Anlo. Others settled in the forested hills and valleys further north. They did not form one kingdom. Each group built its own small state, with its own chief and elders: Peki, Ho, Kpando, Hohoe, and many more. A chief could not simply give orders. He had to listen to his elders and to the people, and a chief who ruled badly could be removed. The states were independent of one another, but they shared a language, a faith, and the memory of Notsie.

pages.alt: Several small towns among green hills, each with a meeting shed and a large shade tree at its centre.

pages.text: Small states are easy to bully. After 1730, the kingdom of Akwamu settled on the eastern bank of the Volta and forced the inland Ewe to pay tribute. This lasted for about a hundred years. Then the states found a leader in Kwadzo Dei, the chief of Peki. In 1833, he brought many of them together in an alliance. Their combined army defeated Akwamu, and the tribute ended. Later, in 1869, an Asante army invaded and did great damage. Again the states had to stand together, and after some years the invaders withdrew.

pages.alt: Chiefs from several towns clasping hands in a circle, with their people gathered behind them.

pages.text: In 1847, a German missionary arrived at Peki at the invitation of its chief and opened a school. More followed. The missionaries learned Ewe, worked out a way of writing it, and printed books in it. Ewe teachers and pastors were trained, and schools spread through the hills. By the early 1900s, the whole Bible had been translated. A written language did more than spread a religion. It allowed people in different towns to read the same words. It gave the Ewe a new sense of being one people, even though they had many chiefs.

pages.text: Then came lines on a map. In 1884, Germany claimed the land east of the Volta hills and called it Togoland. The western Ewe were under Britain. After the First World War, Togoland was itself divided between Britain and France. So the Ewe were split by borders that they had not drawn, and families found themselves in different countries. Many wanted all Ewe lands to be joined together. Others thought it wiser to join the Gold Coast. In the vote of 1956, the majority in British Togoland chose union. In the Ewe south, most voted against it.

pages.alt: A map of the Volta area with two dotted border lines drawn through a region shaded in one colour.

pages.text: British Togoland became part of Ghana at independence in 1957. It is now the Volta and Oti Regions, with parts of others. The borders remain, but so do the ties across them. People still cross to trade, to marry, and to attend funerals. Each year, the Asogli people of Ho celebrate a yam festival that brings together relatives from Ghana, Togo, and Benin. The inland Ewe showed that people do not need a single king to act as one. They need a shared language, the habit of talking things through, and respect for a fair vote.

activities.question: How were the inland Ewe governed?
options: By many small states, each with a chief who had to listen to elders and people

activities.question: What did Kwadzo Dei of Peki achieve in 1833?
options: He united many states and defeated Akwamu
He signed a treaty with Germany

activities.question: Why did writing the Ewe language matter so much?
options: People in different towns could read the same words and feel united as one

activities.question: Apply it: In a class vote on where to go for an excursion, your choice loses. Following the lesson of the article, what should you do?
options: Accept the result of a fair vote, and take part
Demand a new vote every day

activities.prompt: Put these events in order, from earliest to latest.
items: The inland Ewe found many small states
Akwamu forces them to pay tribute
Kwadzo Dei leads the alliance that defeats Akwamu
The people of British Togoland vote to join the Gold Coast
